variant.title: Romans 16:24 and a Blessing Given Twice

spans.text: May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ [be] with you all. Amen.
Ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν.
Ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν.

significance.sourceObservation:
Paul blesses the Roman church at 16:20 — the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you — and then returns to greetings from Gaius, Erastus and Quartus. In some Bibles a second, nearly identical blessing follows at verse 24. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus print it [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition do not [S1, S2, S5]. The two are close but not identical: verse 24 adds "all." In Robinson–Pierpont it also adds an Amen; Boyd's text already has an Amen at verse 20 [C2].

Here the usual shorthand breaks down, and the publishers are the ones who say so. BSB's footnote attributes the verse to "SBL, BYZ, and TR"; MSB's to "SBL, MT, and TR," adding that other critical editions omit it [S1, S3]. SBL is itself a modern critical edition. So this is not a case of the critical editions on one side and the traditional text on the other — modern editors differ among themselves [C3].
significance.interpretation:
As Larry Herzog Jr. observes in *Ad Fontes – Volume One*, this is a benediction doubling one Paul has already given a few verses earlier, and its pastoral weight is essentially nil [C5]. That is the right size for it. The blessing is not in question: it stands at 16:20 in all seven editions on this list [C2]. What differs is whether the closing section of the letter gives it a second time.

The reason it is worth a note anyway is the company it keeps. The publishers report a disagreement among modern critical editions here, and that is more instructive than the verse itself. A reader who has learned to sort Bibles into two camps — old manuscripts against the traditional text — will find the sorting fails here. Editors weigh evidence and reach different judgments, and an edition is a set of decisions rather than a side in a dispute.

What cannot be said from this comparison is which way the doubling ran. That the same blessing appears twice is an observation; explaining how it came to appear twice requires evidence of a kind seven printed editions do not supply.
